## The four o’clock toast

Someone always makes toast at four in the morning. Nobody ever admits to starting it. You go into the staff room for something else and there it is: the smell, the crumbs, someone standing by the toaster as though they’ve only just arrived themselves.

After fourteen years of nights, this is one of the things I’m finding hardest to leave.

I’ve neglected this blog since spring. There isn’t a particularly good explanation for that, and I’m not going to promise to become a regular correspondent now. But on Saturday I did my last ever night shift, and I wanted to put something here about it. Every attempt so far has sounded either like an obituary or the beginning of another piece about the NHS. Nobody has died. I am still going to work. And I’ve written enough about staffing to leave that alone for once.

My last night was Saturday 7 November, nine until half past seven, in majors. From Monday, I’m on a days-only rota.

There are sensible reasons. My knees have views about the work. My sleep has become less something I do than something I keep trying to arrange. My GP has made it clear that my blood pressure is no longer a subject on which I can get away with being vaguely amusing.

I’m forty-two. Folasade, our charge nurse on nights, has been doing them for twenty-two years and still beats me up the stairs. I offer this without attempting to draw any medical conclusions from it.

The change is right for me. I know that. I’m relieved.

I also feel like a traitor for being relieved, which is harder to explain.

***

My first night as an SHO was in 2012. During that first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn’t remember whether I’d given a second dose.

I had. That part was established. It didn’t immediately make me feel better.

I can still remember the frost on the windscreen. Fourteen years later, of all the things my brain might usefully have retained, it has kept that frost.

I don’t want to turn that younger version of me into a story about how doctors are made. I was frightened and tired, and afterwards I sat in a cold car and cried. There wasn’t a lesson I needed to extract from it before I was allowed to go home.

But there were other nights, enough of them that I kept coming back, and eventually the place that had frightened me became somewhere I felt at home.

That happened slowly. I couldn’t tell you when.

There is a particular sort of trust you develop with people you work beside at night. You learn who will notice that you’ve gone quiet. Who can make you laugh when you’re past conversation. Who will ask you to look again, and who you can ask the same of without having to dress it up.

You also become very familiar with one another’s least impressive selves. There is only so much professional polish available at half past five.

For me, nights are when the department is most itself. Fewer managers, more honesty, often more kindness. That isn’t entirely fair to the day shift, which has plenty of all three, including managers who are kind and honest. But at night there seems to be less distance between what needs doing and the people trying to do it. I’ve loved that.

I will miss knowing how to belong there.

***

People often imagine nights in emergency medicine as a succession of dramatic events. There are dramatic events. There are stretches when you’re very busy indeed.

But much of the work is less exciting to describe. It’s listening properly when somebody is telling you something slowly. Explaining again because the first explanation didn’t get through. Remembering that the person in front of you hasn’t had your night; they’ve had their own, and it may have been much worse.

Mostly, it’s about staying kind at five in the morning when you are empty.

I haven’t always managed it as well as I would have liked. I don’t think you can write honestly about fourteen years of this work and claim otherwise. There have been times when my patience was thinner than somebody deserved. Times when I needed a colleague’s kindness before I could find any more of my own.

And sometimes it came from a patient.

An older man once held my hand and told me I had his daughter’s hands.

I’m leaving the circumstances out. They belong to him, and they aren’t needed here. What stayed with me was the unexpected tenderness of it. I was at work, doing my job, and for a moment he saw something familiar in me.

You don’t get to choose which moments you take home. I’m grateful that one came with me.

***

There are things nights took that I was happy enough to give at the time, or thought I was.

There are others I’m less settled about.

I missed both my nieces’ naming ceremonies, even on video, because of nights. My sister in Bangalore never once complained.

I sometimes think a complaint would have been easier to answer. I could have apologised, explained the rota, offered some inadequate defence. Instead she understood. She let me off without making me ask.

The ceremonies happened without me. My nieces are growing up. There isn’t a quieter month in which I can go back and attend.

I don’t want to make a grand account of sacrifice here. Plenty of people work nights. Plenty of people miss things for work, or because of distance, money, illness, all the ordinary difficulties of getting a family into the same place at the same time. I chose this job, and for a long time I chose this way of doing it.

Still, I’m allowed to be sorry about what I missed.

And I’m allowed to admit that my body has stopped accepting the arrangement quite as readily as it used to. I have been slower to accept that than I would recommend to anyone else.

That is probably enough from the doctor who needed her own GP to be firm about blood pressure.

***

I drove home on Sunday morning down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up.

I know. The shipping forecast on catch-up. Apparently I like to be informed about weather that has already happened somewhere else.

I’ve made that drive so many times that it ought to have been unremarkable. But the light was coming up, and I realised I wouldn’t see it from this side of a night shift again.

Of course I’ll be out early again. I haven’t been banned from dawn. But I won’t be coming home from this particular working life, with the department still in my head and the day beginning for everyone else.

I felt sad. More than I’d expected.

I’d assumed that by the time I reached the last drive home, relief would have crowded everything else out. Instead I wanted to get home and sleep, and I wanted the drive to take a little longer.

I’m trying not to argue myself out of either feeling.

***

The department will carry on at night without me. This is obvious, reassuring, and a small injury to the ego.

I’ll still see colleagues. I’ll still work in emergency medicine. I’ll still have difficult shifts and come home tired. Days-only is a change of rota, not a promise that life will suddenly become orderly.

But there will be more chances to say yes to things. More calls to Bangalore when I’m properly awake. Perhaps a bit less negotiating with my own body. I’m looking forward to that, even if I haven’t quite worked out how to leave the nights behind.

I don’t need another fourteen years of them to prove that the first fourteen mattered.

What I hope is that, somewhere around four tomorrow morning, someone gets a few minutes to sit down. That somebody else notices they need those minutes and lets them have them. That the toast appears.

Folasade will know who put it on.

She probably won’t tell.
